question.text: If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y=\sqrt[3] x$ traversed from the point $P(0,0)$ to point $Q(1, 1),$ then $\displaystyle \int\limits_C 4ye^{xy}\,\mathrm{d}x + \mathrm{d}y=$
question.explanation:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y =\sqrt[3] x.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve: \begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j = t^3\,\mathbf{i} + t\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t \in[0, 1] \end{align}

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\,\mathbf j = 3t^2 \, \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}. \end{align}

We can now evaluate the line integral: \begin{align*} \int\limits_C 4ye^{xy}\,\mathrm{d}x + \mathrm{d}y & = \int_{0}^{1} 4ye^{xy} \, \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} \, \textrm d t + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} \left( 4ye^{xy} \, \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)\textrm d t \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} 4t\cdot e^{t^3\cdot t}\cdot 3t^2 + 1 \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} 12t^3 e^{t^4} + 1 \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = \left[ 3e^{t^4} + t \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] & = \left[ 3e^{(1)^4} + (1) \right] - \left[ 3e^{(0)^4} + (0) \right] \\[5pt] & = \left[ 3e + 1 \right] - \left[ 3 \right] \\[5pt] & = 3e - 2 \end{align*}

question.text: The solid enclosed by the hemisphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=2$ for $z \leq 0,$ shown above, can be described in spherical polar coordinates as
question.explanation:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho,\theta,\phi),$ where

  • $\rho \geq 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

  • ${\color{black}\theta}\in [0, 2\pi)$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

  • $\phi \in [0, \pi]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary within the following domains:

  • $\rho \in [0,\sqrt2]$

  • $\theta \in [0,2\pi]$

  • $\phi \in [\pi/2, \pi]$

Therefore, we have

\[ \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\sqrt2}, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2\pi}, \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi/2} \leq \phi \leq \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi} \right\}. \]

question.text: Use Green's theorem to evaluate $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \langle 6x^2-xy+11, y^2 + 1 \rangle$ and $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,-1)$ and $(2,1).$
question.explanation:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that \[ \oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y = \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A. \]

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows: \[ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}} = \oint\limits_{C} (6x^2-xy+11) \, \mathrm{d}x+ (y^2 + 1)\,\mathrm{d}y \]

We have that $P(x,y)= 6x^2-xy+11$ and $Q(x,y)= y^2 + 1.$ Therefore, \begin{align} \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = -x, \qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} & = 0. \end{align}

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows: \[ D = \left\{(x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 2, -\dfrac{x}{2} \leq y \leq \dfrac{x}{2}\right\} \]

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get \begin{align} \oint\limits_{C} (6x^2-xy+11) \, \mathrm{d}x+ (y^2 + 1)\,\mathrm{d}y & = \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \textrm d A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D [0-(-x)] \,\textrm d A \\[5pt] & = \iint\limits_D x \,\textrm d A \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{2} \int _{-x/2}^{x/2} x \, \textrm d y \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} x\big[ y \big]_{-x/2}^{x/2} \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{2} x(x) \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{2} x^2 \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{8}{3}. \end{align}

question.text: Find the average value of the function $f(x,y) = 14xy^2$ on the region $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq y^2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}$ given that the area of the region is $\dfrac{1}{3}.$
question.explanation:
Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

\begin{align*} f_{\textrm{ave}} &= \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)} \iint\limits_D 14xy^2 \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{y^2} 14xy^2 \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{1} \big[ 7x^2y^2 \big]_{x=0}^{x=y^2} \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{1} 7y^6 \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 3\big[ y^7 \big]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\[5pt] &= 3(1 - 0) \\[5pt] &= 3. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the mixed integral \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{y}^{z} (y+z) \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A \] where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by \[ D = \big\{ (y,z) \, : \, 0 \leq y \leq 1, \: y \leq z \leq 3\big\}. \]
question.explanation:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{y}^{z} (y+z) \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A &= \iint\limits_D (y+z)\big[ x \big]_{x=y}^{x=z} \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (y+z)(z-y) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D z^2-y^2 \,\textrm{d}A \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D z^2-y^2 \,\textrm{d}A &=\int_{0}^{1} \int_{y}^{3} z^2-y^2 \: \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left[ \dfrac{1}{3}z^3 - y^2 z\right]_{z=y}^{z=3} \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{3}(27-y^3) - y^2(3-y) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} 9- \dfrac{1}{3}y^3 -3y^2 + y^3\, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} 9- 3y^2 +\dfrac{2}{3} y^3 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\left[ 9y- y^3 + \dfrac{1}{6}y^4 \right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\[5pt] &= 9- 1 + \dfrac{1}{6}-0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{49}{6} \end{align*}
